subject: geography
title: KS3 Geography - Tectonic Hazards
subtitle: Reading practice on tectonic hazards, named examples and risk management.
description: A KS3 reading pack for tectonic hazards. Passages support fact retrieval, inference and explanation using plate boundary processes, case studies and hazard management.

data.sourcePassage: Tectonic hazards are dangerous natural events caused by movement inside the Earth. Most earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and tsunamis happen near plate boundaries, where huge slabs of crust and upper mantle meet. These plates move only a few centimetres each year, but their movement can build powerful pressure. At constructive boundaries, plates move apart and magma can rise to form new crust. At destructive boundaries, a denser oceanic plate may sink beneath another plate, creating earthquakes, volcanoes and sometimes tsunamis. At conservative boundaries, plates slide past each other and can become stuck before suddenly jolting forward.

questions.question: How quickly do tectonic plates usually move each year?

questions.question: Why can slow plate movement still create dangerous hazards?
questions.modelAnswer: Slow movement can build pressure over time, which may be released suddenly.

questions.question: Explain why destructive boundaries can produce more than one tectonic hazard.
questions.modelAnswer: Subduction can build pressure for earthquakes, melt rock to form magma for volcanoes and move the sea floor to create tsunamis.

data.sourcePassage: The impacts of an earthquake depend on both the physical hazard and human vulnerability. Haiti in 2010 had a magnitude of about 7.0, but the death toll was extremely high because the epicentre was close to Port-au-Prince and many buildings were weak. Chile in 2010 had a stronger earthquake of about magnitude 8.8, but far fewer people died. Stronger building standards, preparation and emergency planning helped reduce the death toll. This shows that magnitude is not the only factor that matters. Population density, building quality, wealth, governance, depth of focus and access for rescue teams can all change the impacts.

data.sourcePassage: In 2011, north-east Japan was struck by a very powerful undersea earthquake of about magnitude 9.0. It happened near a destructive boundary where the Pacific Plate is being subducted beneath another plate. The earthquake triggered a tsunami that flooded coastal areas. Japan had strong preparation, including warning systems, earthquake-resistant buildings, evacuation routes and sea walls. Even so, the tsunami caused serious impacts because it was extremely large and overtopped some defences. Roads, ports, railways, power and water supplies were disrupted, and the Fukushima nuclear power station was badly affected.

data.sourcePassage: Volcanoes form where magma reaches the surface through a vent or crack in the crust. Volcanic hazards include lava flows, ash fall, pyroclastic flows, lahars, gases and volcanic bombs. Eyjafjallajokull erupted in Iceland in 2010. Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a constructive boundary where the North American and Eurasian plates move apart. The eruption produced an ash cloud that spread across Europe. Flights were cancelled because ash can damage aircraft engines. People near the volcano were evacuated, scientists monitored the ash, and airlines changed routes and safety rules.

data.sourcePassage: Tectonic hazards cannot be stopped because people cannot prevent plates from moving. However, risk can be reduced through monitoring, protection, planning, education and emergency response. Volcanoes can sometimes be forecast because scientists monitor signs such as small earthquakes, gas emissions, ground swelling and rising temperatures. Earthquakes are much harder to predict exactly, although scientists can identify high-risk areas. Protection may include earthquake-resistant buildings or sea walls. Planning includes evacuation routes, hazard maps and drills. Good management reduces risk, but it cannot remove danger completely, especially when a hazard is very large.
